title: The Nvidia Scandal Could Upend Chip Sales to China. Trump Wants to Keep Them Going
gist: Amid fallout from Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset tied to Megaspeed, Trump is backing Lutnick's cautious export-control stance, believing some chip sales keep China dependent and lift US tech stocks. Rather than blacklisting Megaspeed, which leased Inspur/Aivres-sourced Nvidia H200 compute to Chinese firms from Malaysian and Indonesian data centers, Commerce will issue an interim rule against remote compute access.

insights.claim: President Trump believes allowing sales of some advanced AI chips to China keeps China reliant on US technology while simultaneously boosting US tech stocks, according to sources cited by WIRED.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Policy bias favors continued (non-frontier) Nvidia sales to China; tail risk of a sweeping ban is lower than headlines imply.
insights.quote: allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks

insights.claim: Trump defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's slow export-control action as a way to avoid a blowup with China ahead of a meeting with Xi Jinping, citing a very good current relationship with China.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Diplomatic détente with Beijing is actively suppressing new chip export controls; watch summit outcomes as the key policy driver.
insights.quote: if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China

insights.claim: A senior White House official said Chinese firms cannot acquire Nvidia's most advanced Blackwell and Rubin chips, drawing a line distinct from previous-generation Hopper-based H200 chips.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: The policy red line is at the frontier generation; H200-class China revenue remains politically tolerated while Blackwell/Rubin China upside is off the table.
insights.locator: A senior White House official added

insights.claim: Megaspeed obtained Nvidia advanced AI chips through several layers of companies starting with a subsidiary of Inspur, a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate, per New York Times reporting.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Layered-entity diversion exposes Nvidia and its channel partners to enforcement and reputational risk.

insights.claim: Inspur's California-based subsidiary Aivres could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them to Southeast Asia, transferring billions of dollars' worth, including H200s, to Megaspeed subsidiaries.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Billions in Nvidia sales flowed through a US-domiciled affiliate of a blacklisted firm; tighter affiliate/ownership rules could claw back a meaningful channel.
insights.quote: In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips

insights.claim: Rather than shipping chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers in Malaysia and Indonesia data centers and rented compute power to major Chinese companies, exploiting a remote-access loophole in US export controls.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Southeast Asian data-center capacity is a key conduit for Chinese AI compute; regulation targeting remote access directly hits SEA data-center demand.
insights.locator: Instead of shipping the physical chips

insights.claim: Aivres states it complies with all US export controls, indicating the chip flows may have been legal under the rules then in force.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Legal-loophole framing means remedies will come via new rules rather than penalties on past sales.

insights.claim: At a November 5 Oval Office meeting, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, as Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer had already agreed it should be.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Hawks (Bessent, Rubio, Greer) vs. cautious Commerce signals ongoing policy volatility around China chip controls.
insights.locator: In the meeting, the sources say

insights.claim: Lutnick argued blacklisting Megaspeed would be whack-a-mole because it already held the chips for months, and the real issue is Chinese firms' remote access to US chips.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Entity-list additions alone are ineffective against compute leasing; expect rules targeting cloud/remote access instead.
insights.quote: blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole
insights.locator: Lutnick’s position appears to have been

insights.claim: Trump chose a third path: Lutnick will introduce a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from remotely using advanced AI chips by leasing compute from Southeast Asian data centers.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: An interim remote-access rule is coming; watch SEA data-center operators and cloud providers renting GPUs to Chinese clients for demand hits.
insights.locator: But Trump settled on a third approach

insights.claim: The White House says the new rule will crack down on smuggling of advanced US AI chips and ensure the most advanced chips go first to US AI developers rather than Chinese shell companies.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Framing implies prioritized domestic allocation of frontier chips, supportive of US hyperscaler supply.
insights.quote: help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies

insights.claim: In September 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security began using the affiliates rule, automatically extending restrictions to any company 50 percent owned by an entity-list or military end-user-list firm.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: The 50% ownership rule is the key lever that would capture affiliates like Aivres if revived.

insights.claim: China retaliated against the affiliates rule by suspending exports of critical rare earth metals to the US, prompting internal criticism that Commerce had sparked a trade war.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Rare-earth export bans are Beijing's proven counter to US chip controls; any new tightening raises rare-earth supply risk.
insights.locator: But the move prompted immediate retaliation

insights.claim: After the October 2025 Busan summit trade truce, the White House told Commerce to halt the affiliates rule and pre-clear new export controls, which may have allowed companies like Megaspeed to keep acquiring chips.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: The trade truce effectively loosened chip enforcement; Commerce now acts only with explicit presidential sign-off, making policy hostage to US-China diplomacy.
insights.locator: After the Busan summit at the end
